diagnoses.label: Tokenizable modeled as subtype trait instead of type class
diagnoses.general_pattern: Skill guidance for translating Python `runtime_checkable` Protocol classes to Scala is missing. The idioms file shows Protocols/duck typing as 'no direct equivalent' and points to type classes generically, while the functional file only shows type classes for Show. Nothing explicitly maps `@runtime_checkable Protocol` to a Scala type class with implicit evidence, so the agent oscillated between a `Tokenizable[-A]` type class and a subtype `trait Tokenizable { def toToken: String }`, ultimately choosing subtype dispatch. This loses the structural/ad-hoc polymorphism the Python Protocol expressed and forces user types to extend the trait.
diagnoses.observable_evidence: Trajectory shows the agent first defined `trait Tokenizable[-A] { def toToken(value: A): String }` with an implicit-based `tokenize[A](value: A)(implicit ev: Tokenizable[A])` overload, hit ambiguous-overload compile errors against `tokenize(value: Any)`, then reverted to `trait Tokenizable { def toToken: ***REDACTED*** }` and pattern-matched on it — the agent's own note comments 'mirroring Python's runtime_checkable Protocol' but abandoned the type-class approach because the skills gave no pattern for combining Any-dispatch with type-class dispatch.
diagnoses.missing_reasoning_step: A decision rule for translating `@runtime_checkable Protocol` (structural typing) to Scala: when to use a type class with implicit evidence vs. a subtype trait, and how to reconcile it with an `Any`-based runtime dispatcher (e.g., a `Tokenizable.instanceFor(Any): Option[String]` registry, or restricting the dispatcher to typed overloads).
diagnoses.correct_general_approach: Add explicit guidance mapping Python Protocols to Scala type classes (with `implicit`/`given` evidence) as the default, note the alternative subtype-trait encoding, and warn that combining a type-class overload with an `Any` fallback causes overload ambiguity — suggesting workarounds (distinct method names, prioritized implicits, or a registry keyed by runtime class).

diagnoses.label: No guidance on Any-dispatch overloading pitfalls
diagnoses.general_pattern: The skills describe pattern matching on `Any` and type-class based generics separately, but never warn that mixing `def f(value: Any)` with `def f[A](value: A)(implicit ev: TC[A])` causes ambiguous-overload errors in Scala 2.13. Python's runtime `isinstance` dispatch commonly translates to both styles simultaneously, and the skill omits the interaction.
diagnoses.observable_evidence: Compile errors: 'ambiguous reference to overloaded definition, both method tokenize ... of type [A](value: A)(implicit ev: Tokenizable[A]): Token and method tokenize ... of type (value: Any): Token match argument types (String) / (Int) / (LocalDate) / (Foo)'. The agent had to delete the type-class overload entirely to compile.
diagnoses.missing_reasoning_step: Explicit rule: when translating Python's dynamic dispatch (`isinstance` chains + Protocol matching) to Scala, pick a single dispatch mechanism per method name — either exhaustive pattern-match on `Any`, OR type-class overloads with distinct types — and if both are needed, use distinct method names or a Priority pattern.
diagnoses.correct_general_approach: Document the overload-resolution pitfall and prescribe one of: (a) single `Any`-typed dispatcher that pattern-matches including a `case t: TokenizableTrait` branch; (b) type-class-only API with no `Any` overload; or (c) distinct method names (`tokenize` vs `tokenizeTC`) when both are required.

diagnoses.label: f-interpolator dynamic precision not documented
diagnoses.general_pattern: The syntax-mapping skill shows `f"Value: $x%.2f"` for fixed format specifiers but never explains that Scala's `f""` interpolator requires literal format strings — dynamic precision like `f"$d%.${precision}f"` does not compile. Python's f-string `f"{d:.{precision}f}"` supports embedded expressions in the spec, and the skill provides no equivalent guidance.
diagnoses.observable_evidence: Compile errors on first attempt: 'Tokenizer.scala:177: error: Missing conversion operator in \'%\'; use %% for literal %, %n for newline — case d: Double => f"$d%.${precision}f"' and same for Float on line 178. The agent had to rewrite using `String.format` after the failure.
diagnoses.missing_reasoning_step: A note that Scala's f-interpolator format specifiers must be compile-time literals, and that dynamic precision/width must use `String.format("%." + n + "f", x)` or `"%.%df".format(n).format(x)`.
diagnoses.correct_general_approach: Extend the String Formatting table with a row for 'dynamic precision / width' mapping Python `f"{x:.{n}f}"` to Scala `String.format(s"%.${n}f", x)`, and add a caveat that `f""` specifiers must be literal.

diagnoses.label: Implicit conversions feature-warning not surfaced
diagnoses.general_pattern: The collections and functional skills freely use `implicit` conversions (e.g. `implicit def fromString`) without noting that Scala 2.13 emits feature warnings unless `import scala.language.implicitConversions` is added or `-language:implicitConversions` is set. Agents translating Python union types via implicit lifts hit these warnings.
diagnoses.observable_evidence: Compile output: '4 warnings ... implicit conversion method fromString should be enabled by making the implicit value scala.language.implicitConversions visible.' The agent had to add `import scala.language.implicitConversions` after the fact.
diagnoses.missing_reasoning_step: Guidance that any use of `implicit def ...: T` conversion requires the language import (or compiler flag) in Scala 2.13, and that implicit conversions should be used sparingly for union-type ergonomics.
diagnoses.correct_general_approach: Add a short note in the type-class / implicit conversion sections stating the required `import scala.language.implicitConversions` for Scala 2.13, and recommend preferring explicit constructors over implicit conversions when translating Python union types.

package_assessment.rationale: The failed run's iteration cost and design flip-flops trace to specific gaps in the supplied skills: no explicit mapping for Python `runtime_checkable Protocol` to a Scala type-class encoding, no warning about overload ambiguity when combining `Any` dispatch with type-class overloads, no note about the f-interpolator's literal-format requirement (causing compile errors on dynamic precision), and no mention of the Scala 2.13 `implicitConversions` language import. All are reusable, skill-controllable deficiencies observable in the trajectory's compile errors and reverted designs.
